standard.title: Evaluate patterns and trends
standard.description: evaluate information and data in a range of formats to identify and describe patterns and trends, or to infer relationships
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4S03 (Interpret information displays): Students interpret information and data from a range of sources including maps and timelines. Students can read and describe what information in displays shows.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students evaluate information and data in a range of formats to identify and describe patterns and trends, and to infer relationships between phenomena.

nodes.label: Patterns and trends vs isolated facts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between isolated factual observations and patterns or trends that emerge across multiple data points, and explain what it means to 'identify a pattern' in HASS data.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the difference between an isolated fact and a pattern or trend, using one HASS example.
nodes.typical_width: Explain what patterns and trends mean in HASS contexts — that patterns appear across multiple cases or data points, that trends show change over time — and distinguish these from one-off facts. Apply this understanding to interpret at least one visual data source.
wider: Compare pattern analysis in different HASS disciplines: how patterns are identified in historical evidence versus geographical data versus economic data
Explore how sample size and data completeness affect the reliability of identified patterns — and discuss what makes a pattern convincing versus speculative
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat data as a collection of isolated facts cannot make the inferential move to pattern recognition. Pattern identification is the prerequisite for inferring relationships, which is the central analytical skill in this descriptor.

response_modes.reason: Use a series of data examples where students explicitly name what they see (individual data points) versus what they infer (the pattern across them) — scaffold the inferential move explicitly before applying it to complex data.

success_criteria: Students distinguish between an isolated fact and a pattern or trend in HASS data.
Students identify at least one pattern from a provided data source and describe what it shows.

nodes.label: Reading and analysing graphs and maps
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can interpret data presented in line, bar, column and pie graphs, and extract patterns and trends relevant to HASS investigations.
nodes.minimum_width: Read and describe the pattern shown in one type of graph (e.g. bar or line graph) using HASS data.
nodes.typical_width: Interpret line, bar, column and pie graphs presenting HASS data (e.g. election results, colonial population growth, resource use, economic trends), describing patterns and trends and making simple comparisons between data sets.
wider: Compare data from two different graph types showing the same information, and evaluate which representation makes the pattern more visible
Interpret graphs from First Nations Australians' language and Country/Place data to describe patterns in the diversity and distribution of First Nations peoples

response_modes.reason: Fluency in reading multiple graph types is built through repeated practice — each graph type makes different features of data visible. Students need repertoire across types, not deep expertise in one.

success_criteria: Students correctly read and describe the pattern shown in at least one graph.
Students use specific data values or proportions to support their description of the pattern.

nodes.label: Inferring relationships from visual and written sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine visual and written sources to infer relationships — explaining what a relationship means and how evidence supports it.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one relationship inferred from a visual or written source and explain the evidence that supports it.
nodes.typical_width: Examine photographs, maps and written sources to infer relationships: how drought shapes enterprising behaviour, how place characteristics correlate with settlement patterns, how colonial social structures were shaped by economic roles. Explain how the evidence supports each inferred relationship.
wider: Examine maps and sources showing First Nations Australians' language groups and Countries/Places, and explain the diversity of connections to Country/Place that these sources reveal
Investigate multiple sources on the same phenomenon and compare the relationships each source implies — identifying where sources agree and where they suggest different causal patterns

response_modes.reason: The move from 'observation' to 'inferred relationship' is inferential and requires explicit scaffolding — students need to practise articulating 'I see X, which suggests Y because Z' as a structured reasoning step.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations language and Country/Place maps are a significant and elaboration-supported direction for pattern analysis — examining these sources adds cultural and historical breadth while practising genuine geographic pattern identification.
success_criteria: Students infer at least one relationship from a visual or written source.
Students explain the evidence in the source that supports their inferred relationship.

nodes.label: Evaluating information to identify patterns and infer relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate information and data from multiple formats to identify and describe patterns and trends, and infer relationships, explaining how the evidence supports their analysis.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a pattern or trend and infer one relationship from information in at least two different formats.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate information and data from a range of formats (graphs, maps, written sources, photographs) to identify and describe patterns and trends across a HASS topic, and infer relationships between phenomena with reference to supporting evidence.
wider: Evaluate the reliability of an inferred relationship by checking it against additional sources — and revise the inference where evidence is contradictory
Analyse data showing patterns in a current HASS issue (e.g. environmental change, migration trends, voting patterns) and explain what the patterns reveal about the underlying relationships

response_modes.reason: The integration challenge is moving fluidly across data formats to build a multi-source analytical account — not just reading each source in isolation but drawing on several to construct a coherent analysis.

success_criteria: Students identify at least one pattern or trend from information in multiple formats.
Students infer at least one relationship and explain what evidence supports it.
